read.sections.0.heading.back: One place and an important turning point

read.sections.0.text.note: Wartime occupation of Singapore: kept neutral and close to the English. "Japanese occupation" is written การยึดครองของญี่ปุ่น (not ช่วงที่ญี่ปุ่นยึดครอง from KEY_TERMS) in the reading so the glossary word การยึดครอง appears in both texts; ช่วงที่ญี่ปุ่นยึดครอง is used in the Watch part. Check it reads naturally.
read.sections.0.text.source: On 15 February 1942, British forces surrendered to Japanese forces at the Ford Factory in Singapore. This began the Japanese occupation, which lasted until 1945. Today the factory holds an exhibition about the war, run by the National Archives of Singapore. During the occupation, everyday routines changed. Many schools closed or were used for other things, and many children lost time in class. People did not all live through the same events in the same way. A photo of the building today can show us a place. It cannot show us how people lived there in 1942.
read.sections.0.text.back: On 15 February 1942, the British army surrendered to the Japanese army at the Ford Factory in Singapore. This event was the start of the Japanese occupation, which lasted until 1945. Today this factory has an exhibition about the war, run by the National Archives of Singapore. During the occupation, daily routines changed. Many schools closed or were used for other things, and many children lost school time. Not everyone went through the same events in the same way. A photo of the building today can show us the place, but cannot show how people lived there in 1942.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: On 15 February 1942, British forces gave up Singapore. Japanese forces took control. This was the start of the Japanese occupation. It lasted until 1945. The British gave up in a factory. Today the building has a show about the war. Daily life changed in this time. Many schools closed. Many children missed school. People had different lives. A photo of the building today shows a place. It does not show how people lived in 1942.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: On 15 February 1942, the British army surrendered in Singapore. The Japanese army took control. This was the start of the Japanese occupation. The occupation lasted until 1945. The British surrendered in a factory. Today this building has an exhibition about the war. Daily life changed in this time. Many schools closed. Many children did not go to school. People had different lives. A photo of the building today shows the place, but does not show how people lived in 1942.

read.sections.1.text.source: Singapore's Ministry of Education Heritage Centre writes about schools in this time. It says the Japanese military government made Japanese lessons compulsory in schools in 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese, and they could not use English in school. There was a shortage of food, so many schools grew their own. Gardening became part of lessons. Tapioca, a root that grows easily, became an important food. This source tells us about rules and examples of school life. It does not tell us that every child went to school or had the same lessons. For most children, school almost stopped.
read.sections.1.text.back: The Singapore Ministry of Education's Heritage Centre wrote about schools in this time. It says the Japanese military government made learning Japanese compulsory in schools in 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese and could not use English in school. Food shortages happened then, so many schools grew their own food. Gardening became part of lessons. Tapioca, a root crop that is easy to grow, became an important food. This source tells us about rules and examples of school life, but does not tell whether every child went to school or learned the same way. For most children, school learning almost stopped.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A history centre in Singapore writes about schools in this time. It says Japanese lessons were compulsory from 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese. There was a shortage of food. So many schools grew food. Tapioca is a root plant that grows easily. It became an important food. This source shows us rules. It does not show that every child went to school.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A history centre in Singapore wrote about schools in this time. It says Japanese was compulsory from 1942. Teachers had to learn Japanese. There were food shortages then, so many schools grew food. Tapioca is a root crop that is easy to grow. It became an important food. This source shows us the rules, but does not show whether every child went to school.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Food and the limits of sources

read.sections.2.text.source: Before the war, Singapore bought most of its food from other places. The war cut the ships and trains that brought rice. Lee Geok Boi wrote about wartime food for the National Library in 2019. She used oral history interviews. She explains that every home needed a ration card, and the rice ration got smaller over time. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead of rice. Some food was sold in secret at very high prices, so people with more money could get more. For most people, meals were not enough to stay healthy. To learn about meals then, we need food records or memories, not a photo of the factory now.
read.sections.2.text.back: Before the war, Singapore bought most of its food from elsewhere. The war cut the ship and rail routes that brought rice in. In 2019, Lee Geok Boi wrote about wartime food for the National Library. She used oral history interviews. She explains that every home needed a ration card, and the rice ration kept getting smaller. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead of rice. Some food was sold secretly at very high prices, so people with more money got more food. For most people, the food they got was not enough to keep the body strong. To learn about food then, we need food records or memories, not a photo of the factory today.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Before the war, most food came to Singapore by ship. The war stopped much of the rice. Lee Geok Boi wrote about this in 2019. She used oral history. Each home needed a ration card. Over time, the rice ration got smaller. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes. Some food was sold in secret, for a lot of money. Most people did not get enough food to stay healthy. The photo of the factory does not show what people ate.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Before the war, most food came to Singapore by ship. The war stopped most rice from arriving. In 2019, Lee Geok Boi wrote about this. She used oral history. Each home needed a ration card. Over time, the rice ration got smaller. Many people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes. Some food was sold secretly at very high prices. Most people did not get enough food to be strong. A photo of the factory does not show what people ate.

watch.summary.source: This video is part of a cooking show from Singapore's National Library. A librarian and a guest cook, Lee Geok Boi, make food from the time of the Japanese occupation. First, they talk about the past. There was a shortage of rice in the war. So people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead. Tapioca was easy to grow. The video also talks about rations, and about food that was sold in secret for a lot of money. Then Lee Geok Boi cooks two dishes. She uses only foods that people could get at the time. She makes noodles from tapioca and sweet potato. She also makes boiled tapioca with coconut. The video says tapioca fills you up, but it does not give the body all it needs to stay healthy.
watch.summary.back: This video is part of a cooking show by the National Library of Singapore. A librarian and a guest cook, Lee Geok Boi, cook food from the Japanese occupation. First, the two talk about the past. During the war there was a shortage of rice, so people ate tapioca and sweet potatoes instead. Tapioca is easy to grow. This video also talks about rationing, and food sold secretly at very high prices. Then Lee Geok Boi cooks two dishes. She uses only food people could find then. She makes noodles from tapioca and sweet potato, and makes boiled tapioca with coconut. The video says tapioca fills you up but does not give everything the body needs to be strong.

It is long: the history part runs from about 1:48 to 5:48, and the rest is cooking, so you can stop early. sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson is about a wartime occupation, and some learners have lived through war, conflict or displacement. Never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war or displacement, or about their home country, religion or ethnicity, and never ask them to compare their lives with the people in the sources. Keep the discussion on the sources about school and food, and let any learner step out without giving a reason. The lesson needs no violent images. The occupation also brought killings and harsh punishments; the lesson does not describe them and you do not need to. If learners raise them, say plainly that many people were harmed, then return to the sources. Preview before sharing: the NLB article mentions a harsh punishment in one line, and the video may show photos of starving prisoners of war (from 5:04).

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners describe two different changes in daily life, one about school and one about food, with a source for each, without claiming everyone lived the same way. Evidence move: compare the MOE Heritage Centre's school rules with Lee Geok Boi's food history, then point to the photo's date, 2025, before learners say what it shows. A sound answer gives two different everyday effects backed by sources. Misconceptions to address: "all children attended normal classes", "everyone ate the same food", and the idea that the occupation automatically led to independence later.
educatorNotes.0.back: Goal: learners explain two different changes in daily life, one about schools and one about food, with a source for each, without claiming everyone lived the same way. Evidence method: compare the school rules from the Ministry of Education Heritage Centre with Lee Geok Boi's food history, then point out that the photo's date is 2025 before learners say what the picture shows. A good answer gives two different effects on daily life backed by sources. Misconceptions to address: "every child studied as normal", "everyone ate the same food", and the idea that the occupation automatically led to independence later.

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: the MOE page records rules and examples, not every school. The NLB article draws on the National Archives' oral history interviews (its first Japanese Occupation project, 1981–1985, recorded 179 people); memories are valuable but are one person's account, told decades later. The lesson leaves out the article's ration amounts and prices on purpose. The photo shows the restored building in 2025 with modern flats behind it. If you can get a licensed photo of a wartime ration card with clear provenance, it would make a stronger second picture.
educatorNotes.1.back: Source caution: the Ministry of Education Heritage Centre page records rules and examples, not every school. The National Library Board article uses the National Archives' oral history interviews (the first project on the Japanese occupation, 1981–1985, recorded 179 people). Memories are valuable but are one person's story told decades later. The lesson deliberately leaves out the ration amounts and prices in the article. The photo shows the restored building in 2025 with modern residential buildings behind. If you can find a licensed, clearly sourced photo of a wartime ration card, it would be a better second picture.
